<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, this project is the Dashboard component of the Nezha Monitoring system—a self-hostable, lightweight monitoring and operations tool. It’s a Go-based application that provides a web-based dashboard (both admin and user frontends) along with backend services to manage monitoring tasks like HTTP/TCP/Ping checks, scheduled tasks, alert push notifications, and even a web terminal.

Below is a detailed guide on how to draw the system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Dashboard Frontend:
     - There are two separate “dist” directories under cmd/dashboard (admin-dist and user-dist) which contain the static assets for the admin and user interfaces.
   • Backend API/Controller Layer:
     - Located under cmd/dashboard/controller, this layer contains many Go files (e.g., alertrule.go, jwt.go, oauth2.go, etc.) exposing RESTful endpoints.
   • RPC and gRPC Services:
     - In addition to HTTP controllers, there is an RPC folder (under cmd/dashboard/rpc and service/rpc) to handle remote procedure calls.
     - The proto folder shows Protobuf definitions (nezha.proto) and generated code; these support gRPC-based communications.
   • Service/Singleton Components:
     - The service/singleton directory includes background tasks (e.g., for DDNS updates, scheduled tasks, alert sending, etc.) that run concurrently.
   • Data Model and Utility Libraries:
     - The model folder holds the domain models used by the application, including API and test files.
     - Libraries under pkg (ddns, geoip, i18n, utils, websocketx) support functionalities such as dynamic DNS, internationalization, and HTTP/request wrapping.
   • Development and Deployment:
     - Files like Dockerfile, .devcontainer, and various GitHub workflows indicate containerization and CI/CD.
     - Scripts (in script/) manage bootstrap, configuration, and frontend fetching.
   • Configuration & Internationalization:
     - The service/singleton/frontend-templates.yaml and pkg/i18n indicate theming and language support.

2. Determine Relationships and Data Flows:
   • HTTP Clients (Admin & User Frontends) interact with the Backend API:
     - Requests hit controllers in cmd/dashboard/controller.
     - Controllers call services (such as those in service/singleton for scheduled tasks or state management) and may involve RPC calls.
   • gRPC / RPC Communication:
     - Some components use defined gRPC endpoints (illustrated by protobuf files and the pkg/grpcx) to communicate with other services or internal modules.
   • Utility and Infrastructure services support core functionalities:
     - Packages like pkg/ddns or pkg/geoip are invoked by controllers or services for specific features.
   • Deployment and Containerization:
     - Container configuration (.devcontainer, Dockerfile) and CI/CD workflows help manage build, test, and release pipelines.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Layered Architecture:
     - The project separates concerns among presentation (Frontend distributions), business logic (Controllers and Service/Singleton modules), and data models (Model package).
   • Microservices or Modular RPC:
     - While it’s a monorepo, distinct folders for RPC and singleton services suggest modular internal services interacting via well-defined interfaces.
   • Use of Utility Libraries:
     - The pkg subdirectories encapsulate cross-cutting concerns (e.g., internationalization, ddns, utils).
   • Separation of Concerns:
     - Controllers manage HTTP routing while backend tasks (e.g., scheduling, notification) are handled by service layers.

4. Relevant Technologies, Frameworks, and Libraries:
   • Go Language:
     - The entire code base is written in Go (as seen with go.mod and go.sum).
   • gRPC/Protocol Buffers:
     - The presence of proto files and generated code indicate gRPC communication.
   • Containerization:
     - Dockerfile and .devcontainer files suggest development in containerized environments.
   • CI/CD Integration:
     - GitHub workflows for testing, code analysis, releases, and synchronization.
   • Internationalization:
     - pkg/i18n shows support for multiple languages with translation files in various locales.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram to This Specific Project:
   • For a full-stack monitoring dashboard, emphasize both the frontend (admin & user interfaces) and the backend (API controllers, RPC services, background tasks) components.
   • Clearly delineate the roles of:
       - Frontend: Static asset distributions for admin and user views.
       - Backend REST API: Controllers handling monitoring operations.
       - Internal Services: RPC mechanisms, singleton services for configuration, scheduled tasks, and notifications.
       - Utility Libraries: For functionalities such as DDNS, geoip, and i18n.
   • Include deployment elements such as Docker containers and CI/CD pipelines, as they play a role in the build and deployment processes.

6. Instructions for the Principal Software Engineer Drawing the Diagram:
   • Use a layered diagram:
     - At the top, place “Clients/Users” interacting with “Dashboard Frontend” components (Admin and User UIs).
     - Below that, represent the “Backend API/Controller Layer” (via cmd/dashboard/controller) handling HTTP requests.
     - Show arrows from controllers to “Service/Singleton Components” (background tasks, scheduled jobs, configuration management).
     - Illustrate a separate block for “RPC/gRPC Services” that communicates with both the controllers and internal modules (supported by proto definitions).
   • Separate out “Utility/Library Components” (model, pkg/*) as supporting infrastructure.
   • Denote CI/CD, containerization, and development tools (e.g., .devcontainer, Dockerfile, GitHub workflows) on the side or as an environment context.
   • Use clear labels for each component (e.g., “Frontend (Admin/User)”, “API Controllers”, “RPC Service”, “Background Scheduler”, “Utility Libraries”).
   • Utilize directional arrows to indicate request flow from the frontend to controllers, from controllers to RPC or service layers, and back.
   • Apply color coding or distinct shapes:
       - For example, use blue blocks for frontend components, green for controllers/APIs, orange for background services, and gray for utility libraries/infrastructure.
   • Make sure dependencies (e.g., internationalization, DDNS, geoip) are shown as linked modules that feed into the service or controller layers.

In summary, your diagram should capture all essential architectural elements using a layered approach that separates presentation, business logic, and supporting services/utilities. This detailed diagram will clearly communicate how the Nezha Dashboard manages its responsibilities—from handling HTTP/API requests to orchestrating background tasks and supporting internationalization—all while integrating seamlessly within a containerized and CI/CD-driven deployment environment.
</explanation>
